I hope everyone had a chance to participate in our first ever online monthly meeting last April. It was
a learning experience for all of us, both the participants and those of us pulling the virtual strings behind the scenes. Please send me your comments, complaints and suggestions as we’re still learning
this new meeting format and will continue to make changes and tweaks as we go along.
As you might have guessed, it takes a group of about 4 people in the background, not counting the
presenters, to run the online meetings. To keep the meetings running smoothly, someone needs to
be the greeter and allow people to enter the meeting as they arrive and keep out any cyber intruders.
Someone else needs to control the “spotlight” and ensure that whoever is speaking is stuck on your
screen and not cutting in and out to other participants if they cough or rustle some papers. And yet
another person keeps an eye on the background noises and participant volume levels so they can
mute a participant if they are inadvertently creating background noise. Someone also needs to monitor the Chat screen and bring issues raised in chat to the presenter’s attention when required. And of
course, starting this month, our A/V person needs to control the cameras during the presentations.
Online meetings also require a slightly different etiquette than our physical meetings. For instance, it
is always appreciated if folks mute themselves when not actually speaking. This cuts down the background noise and prevents the main screen from flipping from person to person during general discussions just because someone who is not speaking makes some noise. During presentations it is
best to use the Chat feature to let the presenter know you have a question or comment unless the presenter explicitly encourages people to speak up during his presentation. Of course, you can also use
the Chat feature to make offhand comments and jokes during the presentation without risk of interrupting the presentation.
This month our meeting will return to having our Focus on Fundamentals at the beginning of the
meeting followed by announcements, general business, the main presenter/demonstrator and the
Instant Gallery and President’s Challenge.
After an experimental online meeting among the board members and meeting volunteers, we found
that attempting to have “breakout rooms” for the Tech Talk and Design Discussion groups was just
too unwieldy and confusing for everyone so we’ve decided to run those sessions on a separate evening
for those that are interested. Watch for announcements about those sessions.
For the instant gallery, we’d like to continue the format we tried at our last meeting of people showing off their latest work and briefly telling everyone a bit about it. If you are comfortable doing so, it
is also great if you have photos you’ve taken beforehand that you can show to everyone via the Share
Screen feature of Zoom. Either way, we would really appreciate it if you could take a couple photos of
your pieces and email them to editor@gvwg.ca so that we can include them in the next newsletter.
Screenshots are not of suitable quality for publishing.
I’m looking forward to seeing the projects people have been working on while in isolation during this
month’s President’s Challenge segment of the meeting. I have been spending much more time than
usual in my workshop having a lot of fun experimenting with new stuff, completing a couple of comBy Steve Fairbairn

Editor's Notes
Quarantine disruption continues for all of us so once again we will have to meet electronically via
ZOOM, and, like last month, the credentials for your meeting will be sent via email.
Last month I asked for Isolation Tales and a number of you responded. This issue will be made up
mostly on your stories.
Our regular pre-meeting features were interrupted last time so write-up for those are absent in this
issue. Some effort had been put in to finding a way to do this within ZOOM but after some confusion it was decided that we would have only one pre-meeting event this month and that will be Focus on Fundamentals. The topic will be the Vari-grind jig.
Please continue to share your Isolation Tales as I expect we will be in this unique situation for some
time to come. Send them to editor@gvwg.ca or call me at 604-944-3028.
As Dr. Bonnie says:
Stay Calm. Be Kind. Stay Safe. Together we will get through this.
Bruce Campbell

to

Cindy Drozda to be our

is known for her beautiful finial vessels and
boxes as well as her use of colour and mixed media.
She has produced a number of excellent woodturning videos and travels extensively to demonstrate
and teach. She is a regular demonstrator and panelist at AAW symposia and her work is held in galleries and museums across the USA.

now gives regular on-line sessions from her home

has also provided us with lots of notes and instructions that will be available at a later date.
So mark your calendar and watch for instructions
on how to join her for our June meeting.

I know I’m not alone when I read online about
how this pandemic is affecting the psyche of many
people and I am definitely one of them. Like a lot
of us, I have good and bad days. For me not having the social aspect of my life is causing me issues.
I am fortunate to have many hobbies. Yet, there
are days when motivation is hard to come by.
I spent many hours in my shop, trying to keep
busy with varying degrees of success. There are
certain things that I really don’t like to do and I
always use the excuse I don’t have the time. Well,
now I definitely have the time.
One of my pet peeve’s is making yarn bowls! I
seem to sell them every year but that “J” Hook is
no fun at all. So since I was in a bad mood I figured I would start banging out some of those yarn
bowls in different shapes and sizes. So I start
walking walk out to the wood pile (which is way
too big, and never seems to be getting any smaller), looking for a blank that will make a good yarn
bowl. But, then the internal conversation goes like
this:
“Oh that’s a pretty piece that would make a nice
platter. OK, I will do that. No I am supposed to be
out here looking for yarn bowls! Oh well, I have
lots of time. I’ll squeeze it in.
Staying on track just isn’t happening. Time to sit
down and take a break.
Oh, there’s a burner. I haven’t used that for a
while so let’s play with that.
Now, this is a nice thin piece. Maybe I should be
playing with the piercing equipment. I haven’t
played with that for a while!
Gotta get back on track... back to that wood
shed… remember, yarn bowl!
Oh, there’s that beautiful piece that I thought
would make a wonderful bowl and I’m in the
mood to turn out right now, or there’s another
piece of that would make a yarn bowl! OK I’ll
take them both into the shop.
People are wondering if others are having issues
with this pandemic. The answer is yes. We are being told this could go on for the rest of the year
and we look back at this time we will remember a
very bad time in history. I personally don’t wish to
look back and remember these times. If you spend
a lot of time on the computer as I do and you post
any comments like this you’ll be surprised at how
many people out there can relate.
But, just to prove I’m trying to stay positive here is
a picture of those darn yarn bowls, interrupted by
a platter, interrupted it by a bowl, and anything
else that jumps in front of me!
Gary Burns

In March the City too down a Norway Maple in my
neighbourhood “almost” on my doorstep. I was
left scratching my head how to recover this “gift
horse” as social distancing was coming into effect
across Vancouver and the rest of the country.
Without ready access to a chain saw or trailer and
none of by normal go-to friends to ask to help I
thought I was hooped. While the tree fellers had
bucked the truck into 4 big sections they still
weighted between 200 and 300 lbs each – well and
truly out of my weightlifting class.
They say necessity is the mother of invention. After
about a week of walking by the log the light bulb
when off in my head to try a fridge dolly. Thankfully the local equipment rental store was classified as
an essential service and was still open. So I was in
business. With the help of some levers I was able to
roll 3 of logs off the curb and get them standing
upright before sliding the dolly under.
I did get some pretty strange looks from the neighbours as I made successive trips back and forth
from my house, push the dolly with log down the
middle of the street, but after about an hour of
sweat and grunt work I had recovered 3 out of the
4 logs. The 4th section that included a crotch with
the prospect of some nice fiddleback was going to
be a bridge too far for the fridge dolly. After sleeping on it, I realised that a pallet jack was the answer. Another trip to the equipment rental store
and about 30 mins later the 4th and final piece had
been safely recovered.
While the recovery effort was challenging, processing of the logs into bowl blanks and starting to
turn some bowls has been pure fun. I rented a 20”
gas chainsaw and a 16” electric chainsaw from
Home Depot to cut up the first batch of slabs and
compare the two options before settling on pur-
(Continued on page 7)
by Peter Hill
Recovering a Norway Maple in the Time of COVID-19

chasing a 20” Echo 590 unit. Thanks go out to
Bruce Campbell and Ed Pretty for advice on how
to dissect the logs. This Norway Maple project was
also just the excuse that I needed to invest in a
Oneway Coring system. Again thankfully, Oneway
appears to have been classified as another essential service because I called them up and the unit
was on my doorstep within a week.
As another stroke of luck, our friend Glenn Lucas
from Ireland held a perfectly timed ZOOM demo
with tips and tricks for using the Oneway coring
system. It was a good way to help me christen my
new purchase. If you’re interested, a high definition recording of the demo is available for purchase and download from his website.
So far I have worked my way though about 5
blanks including a couple of 16” x 3.5” bowls this
past weekend and look to have my wood supply
needs covered off for the rest of the COVID 19
shutdown. I just hope the drying process goes as
smoothly.
Mori Kono Carving

Keith has continues to turn out his usual array of
beautiful burl bowls during quarantine time. The
irregular wined bowl pictured below is an example. He said, “It was challenging with the large
open edge wing, keeping it straight and parallel,
with so much 'air' space.” He also mentioned that
he could not use his coring system on this piece so
a lot of that beautiful burl ended up on his shop
floor.
Keith misses the regular Tuesday get-together at
his place with members of both Fraser Valley and
our Guild. Alas, it would seem that a number of
the things we enjoyed in the “before time” will be
on hold for a while longer.
In another project, he was inspired by Larry's Stevenson's presentation at our last in-person meeting and accepted his Display Stand challenge to
make a stand for a large (21" x 2.5") maple burl
platter. After completing the first stand he decided to make a second one and colour it black.
He has been surveying people to see which they
prefer and so far it is about 50/50. It will be interesting to see which of them he settles on or if he
tries something completely different.
Finally, he says, “Thank goodness for our hobbies!” Amen to that.

When one has time available, materials on hand,
and an idea for improvements to the shop’s layout,
plus a COVID self-isolation order, just how will one
keep busy? Yeah, right! Like many of you during
these chaotic times I heard my shop calling. It was
a place to which to retreat. Grounded by fear of
illness and with the encouragement and hard work
of several friends, my shop has been updated with
custom cabinets and counters plus several reused
cabinets from a Craigslist kitchen. I’m retiring
from work in a few months so I took the recent self
-isolation opportunity to rethink and rebuild my
workspace. I’ve been asked to share a bit of the
story with you so here is how I’ve accomplished
about 80% of the project to date. The aim was to
make a personal creative space in which I could
look forward to spending a lot more time, especially as this pandemic moves into its next phases.
Here’s what I came up with.
My basement shop is actually three adjacent
rooms: one main shop room with large tools and
about everything one needs to build or repair almost anything from wood; an outer room with a 5foot workbench, vice, clamp and sheet goods storage plus a finishing area; and an inner room that is
dedicated to woodturning and storing wood
blanks. There’s a 3hp dust cyclone with ducts extending to each room to keep the fine particulates
under control when I’m doing either flat work or
turning. But now instead of piecemeal cabinets
and storage from odd sources that has been added
over many years, the rooms are organized with individually designed Shaker upper and lower storage cabinets and scribed countertops. The timbers
I used to make these were harvested from local
bigleaf maple that a group of friends and I have
sourced and milled and then air dried over many
years. Some is highly figured and/or spalted too,
which has been a real treat to work with. Purpleheart and zebrawood strips with maple hardwood
edges on the countertops have added the kind of
special detail that I appreciate in a workspace. And
attempting to select timbers for side-by-side doors
and drawer fronts that have grain patterns that run
into the next one has been both challenging and a
ton of fun. Wood timbers and stock has been collected for several projects over many years as I was
waiting for the right moment to use it. How interby David Sweet
2020 Workshop Reno - Isolation Tale

esting it’s been that this final shop build for me is
that right moment and project!
If you are like me, you know that our workspaces
are uniquely personal. Plus, ideas, hacks and gadgets, etc. that are incorporated into a shop are inspired from many sources, including from colleagues in the Guild and others with immense experience. Between us there are hundreds of years
of woodworking expertise. When I see other’s
shops and gain ideas from them, then make things
for my own shop in my own way this is some of the
true joy of woodworking for me. I have many people that inspired me plus physically helped me during this project. Current Guild members John
Spitters, Dex Hallwood, Olaf Lepper, Gaalen Erickson, Rick Stuible and Dan Breck, previous members Randy Lane, Rick Friedel and Allan Johanson,
and other friends Tony Spitters, Corry Spitters and
Gerry Ciriani all made immense contributions.
Thank you to everyone for your help! And this
goes out also to all of you Guild members who continually inspire me when I see and appreciate the
outstanding quality of your awesome wood art.

by Steve Hansen

Page 12
GVWG
Was it because of the quarantine or, was it a nice
stretch of weather that set me in motion to perform
a much needed assessment of my wood cache after
35 years of accumulation. Regardless, I pulled everything out, one by one, examining for rot, bugs,
potential objet d’art? There were some surprises as
I assessed each slab, stick, log, root ball, blank,
block, burl, board, tangled mess, and why on earth
did I save that!?! The first batch headed for the
recycle bin/fire pile was 30b.f. of bug infested
Riverview oak logs. I think the unwelcome guests
were imported from Coquitlam. Easy come – easy
go. Aside from one other short log, a walnut, everything else has fared well. I think it helps to have a
lot of red cedar to ward off infections. There was a
bunch of odd-ball stuff that didn’t look too appealing to turn, so they have been relegated to garden
adornments. I also took the opportunity to quickly
taste a dozen blanks on the lathe-usually gnarly
bits of cedars. Some of them show some astonishing character that was not at all apparent from its
exterior. A few others just looked like a whole lot of
trouble for nothing, but will make excellent compost.
It was also a trip down memory lane as I recalled
the circumstances behind some of my acquisitions.
For instance, I have a bunch of large burl slabs
from a chance meeting of a logger, through introducing myself to a beachcomber working the Fraser River during a coffee break. I can’t tell you how
fruitful it can be to mention to everyone you meet
that you are a woodworker. The leads will come. I
also got thinking about tea breaks with my old pal
Art Friesen as I sorted through my lapacho,
guatambu, jacaranda paulista, ibararo, and verawood that he sold me over a few years. Art owned
and ran Montalco, a furniture manufacturer and
also had a sideline importing wood from central
America. A fine woodworker and turner himself
and always seemed to have turned lampshades on
the go. Some of my wood retains scars from a
frightful night after a fire-bug set alight my prime
wood shed. “Your shed is on fire!” blurted by my
wife around 2 A:M one fall night. Out I ran, with
hose in hand and no sooner had I turned it onto
the flames I could hear the welcome sound of sirens - Surrey Fire Service to the rescue. They saved
most of the cache, but there was some loss…
So, I’m all organized again. Was I ever? Perhaps
better now, now that some infected wood is gone
and some new inspirations have surfaced. The exercise was also enjoyable because I like flipping
wood around this way and that, trying to imagine
what on earth is hidden inside – oh the anticipation!

Page 13
GVWG
As a “production” turner I get projects ranging
from a set of wooden pegs 1”d x 14” long to 8’ architectural pillars. These come along quite randomly and over the last year or two they have been
few and far between – until now. Since isolation
started I have had a steady stream of projects with
no end in sight. But, it can be wearing and early
this week I needed a break. So, I declared a
“maintenance day”. It was to be a day where I
fixed stuff in the shop that I had kept putting off.
The list looked like this:
1. Design a 4’ dust manifold
2. Clean out dust collector
3. Replace bag with canister filter
4. Fix wobble in live center
5. Replace burnt out florescent light fixture
6. Replace alligator clip on my sandpaper dispenser for 80 grit
Some other stuff got added on by Shirley but that is
a completely different story.
I got #2, #4 and #5 done and #3 is on order. What
a difference. The light over the lathe is bright! The
live center doesn’t wobble any longer and the draw
on the dust collector is amazing. We all learn to
“work around” things under the pretense that we
will get to them later which often turns to months
and then years.
I am glad that I am busy during self-isolation but I
am
really
happy
with
the
result
of
my
“maintenance day”. Perhaps I need to book one of
them more often and maybe you should too.
Now, I should go and replace that alligator clip and
that dust collector manifold would be really helpful…..
Happy turning, everyone. Be calm. Be Kind. Stay
Safe.
by Bruce Campbell

 Always wear safety goggles or safety glasses that
include side protectors. Use a full face shield for
bowl, vessel, or any turning involving chucks and
faceplates.
 Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder
and wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
 Wear hearing protection during extended periods
of turning.
 Turn the lathe off before adjusting the tool rest or
tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
 Always remove chuck keys, adjusting wrenches,
and knockout bars immediately after use. Never
leave them in place, even for a moment.
 Tie back long hair and avoid loose clothing, jewelry,
or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating
parts or accessories.
 When using a faceplate, be certain the workpiece is
solidly mounted with stout screws (#10 or #12
sheet metal screws as a minimum). Do not use dry
wall or deck screws.
 When turning between centers, be certain the
workpiece is firmly mounted between the headstock driving center and tailstock center.
 Ensure the belt guard or cover is in place.
 Check that all locking devices on the tailstock and
tool rest assembly (rest and base) are tight before
operating the lathe.
 Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
 Rotate your workpiece backwards by hand to make
sure it clears the toolrest and bed before turning
the lathe on.
 Stay clear of the areas directly behind and in front
of the workpiece, they are the most likely areas for
a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good
safety habit is to step out of this zone when turning
on the lathe, keeping your hand on the switch in
case you need to turn the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
 Always check the speed of the lathe before turning
it on. Use slower speeds for larger diameters or
rough pieces and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a
piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always stop the
machine to verify why. As a starting point, consult
your operator’s manual for recommended speeds
for a particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed is
compatible with the size of the blank.
 Exercise extra caution when using stock with
cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets, knots, irregular
shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid
these types of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
 Hold turning tools securely on the toolrest, holding
the tool in a controlled but comfortable manner.
Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
 Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is
possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless
it is securely tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
 Know your capabilities and limitations. An experienced woodturner is capable of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning turners.
 Always remove the tool rest before sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
 Don’t overreach, keep proper footing, and keep
your balance at all times.
 Keep your lathe in good repair. Check for damaged
parts, alignment, binding of moving parts, and other conditions that may affect its operation.
 Keep tools sharp and clean for better and safer perYou mostly turn alone so safety is YOUR responsibility.
Safety Guidelines for Wood Turning

Page 24
GVWG
formance. Don’t force a dull tool. Don’t use a tool
for a purpose for which it was not designed or intended.
 Consider your work environment. Don’t use a
lathe in damp or wet locations. Do not use in presence of inflammable liquids or gases, and always
keep a fully-charged fire extinguisher close at
hand. Keep your work area well lit.
 Stay alert. Watch what you are doing. Pay close
attention to unusual sounds or vibrations. Stop
the lathe to investigate the cause. Don’t operate
machines when you are tired or under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
 Guard against electric shock. Inspect electric
cords for damage. Avoid the use of extension
cords.
 Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn
power off. Don’t leave lathe until it comes to a
complete stop.
 Many accidents to woodturners occur while using
saws, especially band and chain saws. Learn and
follow the safety guidelines for this equipment.
You mostly turn alone so safety is YOUR responsibility.
